title: E-commerce stocks: how to analyze platform companies
description: E-commerce stocks earn the transaction, not the goods. How GMV, take rate and network effects work — with Shopify, Mercado Libre and Airbnb in numbers.
author: AK1A Research Lab
body:
E-commerce stocks are shares in companies that earn their money on digital transactions: marketplaces intermediating purchases of goods (Mercado Libre, Sea Limited), platforms intermediating stays and rides (Airbnb, Uber), and companies selling the tools e-commerce is built with (Shopify). What they share is decisive — the company as a rule does not own the goods being sold. Revenue is a fee on the transaction — changing everything from margin to valuation. This guide walks the mechanics: GMV and take rate, the network effect as a moat, the leverage that turns losses into profits — and why five companies sharing one label trade at a P/E from 15.6 to 94.6.

The examples are five companies from AK1A's analysis universe — Shopify, Mercado Libre, Airbnb, Uber and Sea Limited — with data from public market sources (2026-09-03–16). The guide is delimited against store retail, where goods are owned and their cost sits in the income statement, and against subscription software: the transaction fee takes center stage.

## What e-commerce stocks sell — the transaction, not the goods

The platform's revenue mechanics begin two steps above the income statement. The first number is GMV — gross merchandise volume, the value of everything traded on the platform. The second is the take rate — the share of that volume the company charges for. A worked example: a marketplace intermediating goods worth 10 billion dollars a year at an 8 percent fee earns revenue of 0.8 billion dollars. A retailer with the same volume reports 10 billion in revenue — the cost of goods still to pay. That is why gross margin is a different animal here: the universe's store-retail fashion chains report gross margins around 54–56 percent, while the five platforms span from Uber's 40.8 via Shopify's 47.8 to Airbnb's 82.9 percent. The difference says less about skill than about what each company reports as revenue. Compare platforms on earnings, cash flow and growth — not on gross margin height. How the measure is built and read is covered in [Gross margin](/kurser/v07-bruttomarginal) and [Sales growth](/kurser/v01-forsaljningstillvaxt).

## The network effect — the moat that grows on its own

What should explain why a platform gets to keep its take rate is the network effect: more sellers attract more buyers, more buyers attract more sellers — and every new participant makes the network more valuable to everyone else. It is a moat that grows on its own — unlike the brand, built through years of marketing. The mechanism and its math are covered in [Network effects](/kurser/v15-natverkseffekter); how it is scored in an analysis is shown in [the network effects analysis](/blogg/v15-natverkseffekter-analys). Note the symmetry: the effect works forward and in reverse — if sellers leave, buyers leave with them, and vice versa. Churn on either side is therefore the report's most important early warning. And the moat has a price from the start: Uber's network was deeply loss-making in 2022 — minus 9.1 billion dollars for the year — before volume grew into the fixed costs.

## Operating leverage — when the platform turns

The platform's cost base is comparatively fixed: in principle the same infrastructure serves ten as fifteen billion dollars in volume. That is the mechanics behind the industry's turnarounds — the universe carries three. Uber: from minus 9,141 million dollars in 2022 to plus 10,053 million in 2025. Sea Limited: from minus 1,651 to plus 1,578 million. Shopify: from minus 3,460 million in 2022 to profits in all three following years. The turnarounds share one mechanism: revenues grew into a cost base already built — leverage works both ways. The downside shows in Shopify's 2025 number: revenue grew from 8.9 to 11.6 billion dollars — 30 percent — but earnings fell from 2,019 to 1,231 million. Growth does not guarantee earnings — every cost line is a question to the report, and the reading order is trained in [The quarterly report](/kurser/km-006-kvartalsrapporten).

## Five business models behind the same label

The label e-commerce stocks hides five different ways of earning money. **Shopify** sells the tools: software and payment flows to other people's stores, with a gross margin of 47.8 percent and a balance sheet almost without debt — a debt-to-equity ratio of 0.01. **Mercado Libre** is the marketplace that became a bank: revenue grew from 10.8 to 28.9 billion dollars 2022–2025, 38.9 percent per year, but the debt-to-equity ratio of 1.69 carries a lending operation — that side of the company is analyzed as a financial company, see [Debt-to-equity](/kurser/v10-skuldsattningsgrad). **Airbnb** is the purest marketplace: gross margin 82.9 percent, ROE 34.5 percent and a free cash flow that in 2025 was 1.85 times earnings — 4,646 against 2,511 million dollars. **Uber** is the transport network: 52.0 billion dollars in revenue, 9.8 billion in free cash flow — and the lowest multiple of the five. **Sea Limited** carries three legs — e-commerce, entertainment, financial services — with the universe's highest growth rate: 48.1 percent over the latest twelve months, but an FCF margin of only 0.2 percent. As a contrast: Amazon, the most capital-intensive giant of the universe's technology branch with 2,680 billion dollars in market value, therefore reports an FCF margin of minus 1.5 percent — inventory and logistics tie up capital the lighter platforms avoid. The difference between the business models is thus not a footnote but the analysis itself, and the craft of segment reporting is trained in [Revenue diversification](/kurser/v03-intaktsdiversifiering).

## Valuation — from 15.6 to 94.6 in the same industry

The P/E figures of the five: Uber 15.6, Airbnb 38.1, Sea 43.6, Mercado Libre 49.8, Shopify 94.6 — more than sixfold between the extremes. What the market prices becomes clear: the growth rate. Sea and Mercado Libre grow fastest (48.1 and 46.0 percent respectively), Shopify carries 33.7, Uber 16.7. To capture multiple and growth in a single number, reach for PEG — Sea 1.15, Airbnb 1.42, Shopify 2.61, Mercado Libre 3.4 — but the number has documented weaknesses as a sorting list, see [the PEG multiple's weaknesses](/blogg/peg-multipeln-svagheter-2026) and [the PEG course](/kurser/km-027-pegratio). Two reservations: the FCF yield spans from 13.4 percent (Mercado Libre) to 0.9 (Shopify), but in the first case financial-services flows mix in — customer funds are not distributable cash. And when the earnings denominator falters, [the P/S ratio](/blogg/ps-tal-nar-ar-det-anvandbart) with the course [P/S](/kurser/v04-ps) is the complement; the P/E measure itself is deepened in [the P/E deep dive](/kurser/km-009-pe). The comparison medians are in [the industry medians](/blogg/branschmedianer-akm2).

## Five points for reading the report

- **GMV, active users and take rate** — revenue divided by volume shows whether the platform raises the fee, grows on volume or both; the trend is the business model's pulse.
- **The segments one by one** — Sea and Mercado Libre carry finance legs, Uber splits rides and deliveries; the group aggregate hides more than it reveals, see [the revenue diversification analysis](/blogg/intaktsdiversifiering-risken-som-inte-syns-i-pe).
- **Cash flow against earnings** — Airbnb's 1.85 times and Sea's 0.2 percent FCF margin are the same exercise from opposite ends: does the cash flow follow the income statement? The craft lives in [The cash flow analysis](/kurser/km-003-kassaflodesanalysen).
- **Credit losses where there is fintech** — the debt-to-equity ratio of 1.69 at Mercado Libre is business model, not accident; credit cost as a share of revenue is the line to follow.
- **One-off items and notes** — Airbnb's earnings fell from 4,792 million dollars in 2023 to 2,648 million in 2024 while revenue grew; such breaks are explained in the notes, and the routine is trained in [Notes — the hidden information](/kurser/km-004-noter).

## The summary

- Revenue is the transaction fee: 10 billion dollars in volume at a take rate of 8 percent gives 0.8 billion in revenue — without cost of goods.
- The gross margin spans 40.8–82.9 percent among the five; the level reflects the accounting, not the skill.
- Leverage turns: Uber from minus 9,141 million dollars in 2022 to plus 10,053 million in 2025; Sea and Shopify turned the same year.
- The multiple span P/E 15.6–94.6 prices the growth rate 16.7–48.1 percent; PEG compares — with known weaknesses.
- The FCF yield is not compared flat out: finance legs and customer funds make 13.4 and 0.9 percent different things.

The continuation track: the course [Network effects](/kurser/v15-natverkseffekter) deepens the moat, [the network effects analysis](/blogg/v15-natverkseffekter-analys) shows the scoring in practice, and [the complete guide to Swedish stock analysis](/blogg/komplett-guide-svensk-aktieanalys-2026) sets the method in the whole.

_This is educational financial analysis, not investment advice._
